A huge complex of earthen mounds and ridges in northeast Louisiana, built between about 1700 and 1100 BCE. Six curved ridges, one inside the other, face a bayou, with large mounds around them. Mound A is one of the biggest earthworks in North America, and it seems to have gone up within a few months.

What makes it remarkable is who built it: hunter-gatherers and fishers, not farmers. They lived on fish, game, nuts and seeds, with only a small part from the plants of the Eastern Agricultural Complex.

Trade reached far. Copper from the Great Lakes and stone from the Appalachians and the Ozarks came to the site, probably along the Mississippi and its rivers. The area has no stone, so people cooked with fired clay balls, found there by the thousands.

Poverty Point came more than a thousand years before the mound towns of Hopewell and Cahokia, and in the same centuries as the first Olmec centres in Mexico. It became a World Heritage Site in 2014.
